title: Psalms Chapter 73 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Psalms chapter 73 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Psalms Chapter 73 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Psalms Chapter 73.

questions.question: In Psalms 73, which of the following appears FIRST in the chapter?
options: The eyes of the wicked stand out with fatness
Pride compasseth the wicked about as a chain
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:1 states 'Truly God is good to Israel...' which is the earliest event mentioned among the options.

questions.question: According to Psalms 73:1, to whom is God good?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:1 states, 'Truly God is good to Israel...' indicating God is good to Israel.

questions.question: In Psalms 73:2, what nearly happened to the psalmist's feet?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:2 states, 'my feet were almost gone;' showing the psalmist's feet nearly failed him.

questions.question: What caused the psalmist to be envious, according to Psalms 73:3?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:3 says, 'For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.'

questions.question: According to Psalms 73:4, what is said about the death of the wicked?
options: There are no bands in their death
questions.correctAnswer: There are no bands in their death
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:4 states, 'For there are no bands in their death:' indicating their death is without bonds or restraints.

questions.question: What does Psalms 73:5 say about the troubles of the wicked?
options: They are not in trouble as other men
They are plagued like other men
questions.correctAnswer: They are not in trouble as other men
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:5 says, 'They are not in trouble as other men;' showing the wicked don't experience trouble like others.

questions.question: According to Psalms 73:6, what surrounds the wicked like a chain?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:6 states, 'Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain;' indicating pride surrounds them like chains.

questions.question: What covers the wicked as a garment, according to Psalms 73:6?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:6 says, 'violence covereth them as a garment;' showing violence covers them like clothing.

questions.question: What do the eyes of the wicked stand out with, according to Psalms 73:7?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:7 states, 'Their eyes stand out with fatness;' indicating their eyes protrude due to abundance.

questions.question: According to Psalms 73:8, what kind of speech do the wicked use?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:8 says, 'They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression;' describing their speech.

questions.question: In Psalms 73:9, what do the wicked set their mouth against?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:9 states, 'They set their mouth against the heavens;' indicating their defiance toward God.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 73:1 says God is good to those who have a clean heart.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:1 states, 'Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.'

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 73:5 mentions that the wicked are not plagued like other men.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:5 says, 'neither are they plagued like other men,' confirming this fact.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 73:10 says the wicked receive waters of a full cup.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:10 says 'Therefore his people return hither: and waters of a full cup are wrung out to them,' referring to God's people, not the wicked.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 73:3 states the psalmist was envious of the righteous.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:3 states the psalmist was envious of the foolish, when he saw the prosperity of the wicked, not of the righteous.

medium.title: Psalms Chapter 73 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Psalms Chapter 73 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What do the ungodly say about God's knowledge?
questions.explanation: This is correct because Psalms 73:11 states, 'And they say, How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?'

questions.question: What does Psalms 73:12 say about the ungodly?
questions.explanation: This is supported by Psalms 73:12, which states, 'Behold, these are the ungodly, who prosper in the world; they increase in riches.'

questions.question: What did the psalmist feel about cleansing his heart?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:13 mentions, 'Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency.'

questions.question: What is the psalmist's experience every morning according to Psalms 73:14?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:14 states, 'For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning.'

questions.question: What did the psalmist fear if he spoke out his feelings?
options: He should offend against the generation of thy children.
questions.correctAnswer: He should offend against the generation of thy children.
questions.explanation: This is derived from Psalms 73:15, which states, 'If I say, I will speak thus; behold, I should offend against the generation of thy children.'

questions.question: What was too painful for the psalmist to understand?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:16 indicates, 'When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me;' referring to the struggle to understand the prosperity of the wicked.

questions.question: What did the psalmist realize upon entering the sanctuary of God?
questions.explanation: This understanding is described in Psalms 73:17, 'Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end.'

questions.question: What did God do to the ungodly according to Psalms 73:18?
options: He set them in slippery places.
questions.correctAnswer: He set them in slippery places.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:18 states, 'Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction.'

questions.question: How are the ungodly described in Psalms 73:19?
questions.explanation: This description is found in Psalms 73:19, which says, 'they are utterly consumed with terrors.'

questions.question: What analogy does the psalmist use to describe the fate of the ungodly in Psalms 73:20?
options: Like a dream when one awaketh.
questions.correctAnswer: Like a dream when one awaketh.
questions.explanation: This is stated in Psalms 73:20, 'As a dream when one awaketh; so, O Lord, when thou awakest, thou shalt despise their image.'

questions.question: What does the psalmist conclude about God’s goodness in Psalms 73:1?
options: God is only good to the wealthy.
Truly God is good to Israel.
questions.correctAnswer: Truly God is good to Israel.
questions.explanation: This is affirmed in Psalms 73:1, 'Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart.'

questions.question: What did the psalmist experience when he looked at the prosperity of the wicked in Psalms 73:3?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:3 states, 'For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.'

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist believed that the ungodly faced many troubles.
questions.explanation: The psalmist notes that 'They are not in trouble as other men.' (Psalms 73:5), indicating that he observed they do not face the same troubles as the righteous.

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist felt that cleansing his heart was a worthwhile endeavor.
questions.explanation: He expressed in Psalms 73:13, 'Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain,' indicating he felt it was not worthwhile.

questions.question: True or False: The ungodly are described as having no pride or violence.
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:6 states, 'Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; violence covereth them as a garment,' indicating they are indeed marked by pride and violence.

hard.title: Psalms Chapter 73 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Psalms Chapter 73.

questions.question: What was the emotional state of the psalmist as described in Psalms 73:21?
questions.explanation: The psalmist states, 'Thus my heart was grieved,' indicating a state of deep emotional distress (Psalms 73:21).

questions.question: How does the psalmist describe his previous understanding of his situation in Psalms 73:22?
questions.explanation: The psalmist admits, 'So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee,' showing his recognition of his prior lack of understanding (Psalms 73:22).

questions.question: According to Psalms 73:23, what reassurance does the psalmist have regarding his relationship with God?
questions.explanation: The psalmist declares, 'Nevertheless I am continually with thee,' affirming the constancy of God's presence in his life (Psalms 73:23).

questions.question: What does God provide for the psalmist according to Psalms 73:24?
questions.explanation: The verse states, 'Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory,' indicating both guidance and a promise of glory (Psalms 73:24).

questions.question: In Psalms 73:25, what question does the psalmist ask regarding his desire?
options: Whom have I in heaven but thee?
Is there anyone to help me?
questions.correctAnswer: Whom have I in heaven but thee?
questions.explanation: The psalmist expresses a profound desire for God alone, stating, 'Whom have I in heaven but thee?' (Psalms 73:25).

questions.question: What does the psalmist claim is the strength of his heart in Psalms 73:26?
questions.explanation: The psalmist acknowledges, 'but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever,' emphasizing God's role as his source of strength (Psalms 73:26).

questions.question: What does the psalmist state about those who are far from God in Psalms 73:27?
questions.explanation: The psalmist warns, 'For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish,' indicating the fate of the ungodly (Psalms 73:27).

questions.question: What is the meaning of the Hebrew word 'reins' in Psalms 73:21?
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word for 'reins' (כְּלָיוֹת, kilyot) refers to the kidneys, historically associated with feelings and emotions, as seen in Psalms 73:21.

questions.question: Which literary device is primarily employed in Psalms 73:27?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:27 employs parallelism, contrasting 'they that are far from thee' with their fate of perishing, emphasizing the moral lesson.

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of seeking God as expressed in Psalms 73:28?
questions.explanation: Matthew 6:33 encourages seeking first the kingdom of God, echoing the psalmist's theme of drawing near to God (Psalms 73:28).

questions.question: Which other Bible passage connects to the theme of guidance as mentioned in Psalms 73:24?
questions.explanation: Proverbs 3:5-6 speaks of trusting in the Lord for guidance, paralleling the psalmist's declaration of God's counsel (Psalms 73:24).

questions.question: What precedes the statement in Psalms 73:21?
questions.explanation: The verse preceding Psalms 73:21 discusses God's goodness to Israel, setting the context for the psalmist's grief (Psalms 73:1).

questions.question: What does Psalms 73:14 indicate about the psalmist's daily experience?
questions.explanation: The psalmist expresses, 'For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning,' indicating his daily struggles (Psalms 73:14).

questions.question: Is it true that the psalmist believes it is good to draw near to God as stated in Psalms 73:28?
questions.explanation: The psalmist concludes that 'it is good for me to draw near to God,' affirming the value of closeness to God (Psalms 73:28).

questions.question: Is it false that the psalmist expresses a desire for earthly riches in Psalms 73:25?
questions.explanation: The psalmist explicitly states that there is 'none upon earth that I desire beside thee,' showing his lack of desire for earthly riches (Psalms 73:25).

theological.title: Psalms Chapter 73 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Psalms Chapter 73 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What doctrine does Psalms 73:1 teach about God's nature?
options: God is good to Israel and to the clean in heart
God is indifferent to human righteousness
God rewards the wicked more than the righteous
God's goodness is conditional upon human works
questions.correctAnswer: God is good to Israel and to the clean in heart
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:1 states, 'Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart,' affirming the doctrine of God's goodness especially toward His covenant people and those who are pure in heart.

questions.question: What doctrine concerning human sin does Psalms 73:3 illustrate?
options: Envy arises from observing the prosperity of the wicked
Sin is irrelevant to earthly success
God approves of envy in the righteous
questions.correctAnswer: Envy arises from observing the prosperity of the wicked
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:3 shows the psalmist's envy toward the foolish because of their worldly prosperity, teaching that human sin can manifest as envy when one perceives the wicked prospering.

questions.question: What doctrine regarding divine justice is taught in Psalms 73:18?
options: God ultimately brings the wicked down to destruction
God ignores the end of the wicked
The wicked are preserved by God indefinitely
God's justice is postponed without consequence
questions.correctAnswer: God ultimately brings the wicked down to destruction
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:18 states, 'Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction,' affirming the doctrine that God's justice ensures the final downfall of the wicked.

questions.question: Which divine attribute does Psalms 73:10 specifically demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:10 indicates God's knowledge and control over the fate of His people and the wicked, revealing His omniscience in overseeing justice.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is demonstrated in Psalms 73:24?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:24 says, 'Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel,' emphasizing God's attribute of guidance for His people.

questions.question: How does Psalms 73 prepare for themes in the New Testament concerning suffering and vindication?
options: By expressing the psalmist’s struggle with the prosperity of the wicked and ultimate trust in God’s justice
By denying the reality of suffering for the righteous
By teaching that all suffering is due to personal sin
By promising earthly riches to the faithful
questions.correctAnswer: By expressing the psalmist’s struggle with the prosperity of the wicked and ultimate trust in God’s justice
questions.explanation: The psalm’s arc of wrestling with envy and concluding in trust aligns with New Testament themes, such as in Hebrews 12, about enduring suffering and trusting God's righteous judgment.

questions.question: In what way does Psalms 73 connect to redemptive-historical themes of sanctification?
options: It portrays sanctification as a process of understanding God's justice and drawing near to Him
It claims sanctification is instantaneous and effortless
It denies the importance of sanctification
It equates sanctification with earthly success
questions.correctAnswer: It portrays sanctification as a process of understanding God's justice and drawing near to Him
questions.explanation: Verses 17 and 28 emphasize gaining insight in God's sanctuary and drawing near to God, indicating sanctification as growth in understanding and relationship with God.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 73:13 and 73:14 teach about the experience of righteousness and suffering?
options: Righteous living does not guarantee exemption from suffering
Suffering indicates divine rejection of the righteous
questions.correctAnswer: Righteous living does not guarantee exemption from suffering
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:13 and 14 express the psalmist’s personal innocence yet continual suffering, teaching that righteousness does not always result in immediate relief from affliction.

questions.question: What combined doctrine do Psalms 73:25 and 73:26 teach about the believer's ultimate hope?
options: God alone is the believer’s eternal desire and strength
The believer’s hope is in earthly possessions
The believer finds ultimate satisfaction in human relationships
questions.correctAnswer: God alone is the believer’s eternal desire and strength
questions.explanation: Verses 25 and 26 emphasize the psalmist’s exclusive desire for God and God as the strength and portion forever, affirming God as the believer’s ultimate hope.

questions.question: What combined doctrine about divine judgment and human folly is taught in Psalms 73:21 and 73:22?
options: Human ignorance leads to grief, but God’s judgment reveals true wisdom
Grief is unrelated to understanding divine justice
Divine judgment is arbitrary and unknowable
questions.correctAnswer: Human ignorance leads to grief, but God’s judgment reveals true wisdom
questions.explanation: Verses 21 and 22 describe the psalmist’s grief and foolishness prior to understanding God’s judgment, illustrating how divine revelation corrects human folly.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that Psalms 73:16-20 teaches God is unjust because the wicked prosper. What does this passage actually teach?
options: It teaches that, upon reflection in God's sanctuary, the ultimate fate of the wicked is destruction, affirming divine justice
It claims the wicked will prosper forever without consequence
It denies any reality of future judgment
It says God is unaware of the wicked’s actions
questions.correctAnswer: It teaches that, upon reflection in God's sanctuary, the ultimate fate of the wicked is destruction, affirming divine justice
questions.explanation: Verses 16-20 show the psalmist’s initial confusion but ultimate understanding that God will bring the wicked down suddenly, demonstrating God's just judgment.

questions.question: What doctrine about human dependence on God is taught in Psalms 73:23?
options: The believer is continually supported by God's presence
The believer is abandoned by God in trials
Human strength is sufficient without divine aid
God occasionally helps but is mostly distant
questions.correctAnswer: The believer is continually supported by God's presence
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:23 states, 'Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand,' affirming constant divine support.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is highlighted in Psalms 73:27 regarding those far from God?
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:27 says, 'For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish,' showing God's justice in dealing with those who turn away from Him.

questions.question: How do Psalms 73:4 and 73:5 together illustrate the theological problem of the prosperity of the wicked?
options: They describe the wicked as free from death’s bonds and trouble, intensifying the psalmist’s struggle with divine justice
They deny the prosperity of the wicked
They claim the wicked suffer more than the righteous
They indicate the wicked lack any worldly strength
questions.correctAnswer: They describe the wicked as free from death’s bonds and trouble, intensifying the psalmist’s struggle with divine justice
questions.explanation: Verses 4 and 5 emphasize the apparent immunity of the wicked to death and trouble, which challenges the psalmist's understanding of justice.

questions.question: What narrative arc concerning trust and declaration is found in Psalms 73:28?
options: Drawing near to God leads to trust and the desire to proclaim His works
Trust in God is unrelated to declaring His works
Declaring God’s works is only for the righteous elite
Drawing near to God results in silence and doubt
questions.correctAnswer: Drawing near to God leads to trust and the desire to proclaim His works
questions.explanation: Psalms 73:28 concludes, 'But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works,' linking nearness to God with trust and testimony.
